questions.q: Which of these is the best description of reference data?
options: A record describing a specific business event, like an order or a case
A controlled list of values used to validate or categorize other data, like country codes or status values
Any data stored in a custom object
Data that only exists in an external ERP system
questions.explain: Reference data is the vocabulary other data is validated against or categorized by -- country codes, currency codes, status values -- distinct from master data (the subject of a record) and transactional data (business events).

questions.q: A company's 'Industry' field is free text in Salesforce, a governed picklist in the ERP, and a separate list in a marketing tool, producing three different answers to 'what's our largest industry segment?' What is the root cause?
options: The underlying customer base is genuinely changing industries quickly
Salesforce cannot store picklist values
Each system's reference data disagrees about what the valid categories even are
Reports can only be run from one system at a time
questions.explain: This is a classic standardization failure: the systems don't disagree about the customers, they disagree about the reference-data categories themselves, so the same underlying data gets bucketed differently in each report.

questions.q: Does standardizing a reference-data list across systems require physically merging it into one shared database table?
options: Yes, standardization is impossible without a single shared table
No -- it requires agreement on the authoritative values and a documented process for keeping each system's copy in sync
Yes, but only for currency codes specifically
No -- standardization is purely a reporting-layer concern and never touches the source systems
questions.explain: Standardization is about agreement on meaning and a sync process (often a crosswalk), not about forcing every system to share physical storage.

questions.q: A reference list needs structured attributes -- codes with descriptions and effective dates -- and should be deployable like code across environments. Which Salesforce mechanism fits best?
options: A standard picklist
A custom metadata type
A plain text field with validation rules only
Chatter
questions.explain: Custom metadata types support structure beyond a flat value list and are deployable across environments, unlike a standard picklist which is a simpler flat list of values.

questions.q: Why does reference data still need a named owner, even though it feels smaller and less important than master data?
options: It doesn't -- reference data is exempt from governance by definition
Because Salesforce automatically governs all picklist changes without human approval
Because an ungoverned change, like silently adding a new category value, can break downstream reporting without anyone noticing until numbers stop reconciling
Because only System Administrators are capable of editing picklists
questions.explain: Reference-data changes are quiet but high-impact -- an unannounced addition or renaming of a value can silently break historical comparisons in every report that segments by that list, which is exactly why it needs an owner and a change process.
